title: Rent-a-Room Tax Limit Rises to 16,000 Euro
summaryZh: 房間出租免稅上限從一萬四調高到一萬六歐元，盼增加學生床位。
paragraphs: People in Ireland who rent out a room in their own home will soon be able to earn more money without paying tax on it. In Budget 2027, the Government raised the tax-free limit of the rent-a-room scheme from 14,000 euro to 16,000 euro a year. It is the first increase since 2017.

The scheme has become much more popular in recent years. The number of people claiming the relief almost doubled between 2020 and 2024, rising from about 9,300 to more than 18,000. Universities say the number of rooms offered to students in family homes has also grown, from around 2,000 in 2022 to over 5,000 this year.
However, there is an important rule to remember. If a homeowner earns even slightly more than the limit, all of the rental income becomes taxable, not just the extra amount.

Ministers argue that the change will make more beds available quickly, without any need for planning permission or new construction. The scheme will now also cover small cabins built in a homeowner's garden, although this part of the plan has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians.

People in Ireland who rent a room in their home to someone can soon earn more money without paying tax. In Budget 2027, the Government raised the tax-free limit of the rent-a-room scheme from 14,000 euro to 16,000 euro a year. This is the first rise since 2017.

More and more people use the scheme. Between 2020 and 2024, the number of people using it almost doubled, from about 9,300 to more than 18,000. Universities say that more families now offer rooms to students too, from about 2,000 rooms in 2022 to over 5,000 this year.
But there is one important rule. If you earn even a little more than the limit, you must pay tax on all of the money, not only the extra part.

Ministers say the change will give students more beds quickly, without building new houses. The scheme will now also include small wooden cabins in people's gardens, but opposition politicians do not like this part of the plan.

Homeowners in Ireland who let a room in their own property will soon be able to earn more before incurring any tax. Budget 2027 raised the tax-free threshold of the rent-a-room scheme from 14,000 euro to 16,000 euro a year, the first adjustment since 2017.

Uptake of the scheme has surged in recent years. The number of claimants almost doubled between 2020 and 2024, climbing from about 9,300 to over 18,000. Universities report a parallel rise in so-called digs, with rooms offered to students in family homes increasing from around 2,000 in 2022 to more than 5,000 this year.
There is, however, a significant catch. Should a homeowner's income exceed the threshold by even a small margin, the entire rental income becomes taxable, not merely the surplus.

Ministers argue the measure will swiftly free up beds without the need for planning permission or fresh construction. The scheme is also being extended to cover modular cabins in homeowners' gardens, a provision that has drawn fierce criticism from opposition politicians.

Irish homeowners who rent out a room within their residence will shortly be permitted to earn a higher income without incurring taxation. In Budget 2027, the Government increased the tax-exempt threshold of the rent-a-room scheme from 14,000 euro to 16,000 euro annually, representing the first revision since 2017.

Participation in the scheme has risen substantially. Between 2020 and 2024, the number of claimants almost doubled, increasing from approximately 9,300 to in excess of 18,000. Higher education institutions also report a considerable expansion in student accommodation within family homes, from roughly 2,000 rooms in 2022 to more than 5,000 at present.
Nevertheless, a crucial stipulation applies. Should a homeowner's earnings marginally exceed the limit, the entirety of the rental income becomes liable to tax, rather than solely the excess amount.

According to ministers, the policy will generate additional accommodation rapidly, without necessitating planning permission or new construction. The scheme has also been extended to encompass small cabins in homeowners' gardens; however, this element has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians.
